title: Logan argues for at least two more rate increases to move policy into restrictive territory
summary: Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan judged on November 10 that the federal funds target range was at least half a percentage point below a level that would begin to restrain demand sufficiently. She favoured at least two further quarter-point increases, followed by a pause to assess the effects. In her view the October decision to skip a rate increase after September’s quarter-point move accommodated unusually volatile markets without changing the appropriate destination. She allowed that increases could come faster over the winter. This was her assessment of the economic outlook and the appropriate response, conditional on incoming evidence, rather than a commitment by the FOMC.

Logan saw ample demand and a broadly balanced labour market. Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter and the Dallas Fed’s weekly index was consistent with roughly 3% growth. She attributed resilient consumption partly to stock-market gains for wealthier households and took reassurance from upward revisions to household income data. Business equipment investment was 14% higher than a year earlier. Computers, peripherals and communications equipment accounted for over 80% of that increase, while investment appeared to be spreading to the equipment used to manufacture chips, generate power and transmit electricity. Employers’ reluctance both to shed staff and to hire made job search difficult, yet unemployment just above 4% and payroll gains exceeding trend labour-force growth suggested to her that maximum employment had been reached (economic activity and employment section).

Logan’s case for tighter policy rested on the breadth and persistence of price pressure. Headline PCE inflation was 3.6% through September and core inflation 3.1%. She expected some energy and tariff-sensitive goods pressures to dissipate. Prices for core services excluding housing and transportation, however, rose 3.2%, eight tenths above the pace historically consistent with the inflation target. The New York Fed’s multivariate core trend was 2.8% and the Dallas Fed’s trimmed mean was 2.3%. She gave less weight to the latter because staff research suggested the current mix of price changes caused the method to discard too many increases. A manufacturer’s intention to compensate employees for past inflation illustrated a possible route to persistence. It was a single business contact’s view, not evidence of widespread wage acceleration (inflation and monetary policy sections).

The policy stance itself depended on the inflation expectation used. Across thirteen surveys, staff judged expected near-term PCE inflation to be around 3.1%. Subtracting that from the 3.88% nominal federal funds rate gave a real rate of about 0.78%, below the 1–1.85% range of neutral real rates across eight models. Neutral is unobservable. Logan also cited relatively tight credit spreads, rising stocks and banks’ willingness to lend. Ten-year Treasury yields had risen roughly three quarters of a percentage point during 2026. She interpreted much of that move as investors expecting stronger nominal growth and a higher neutral rate, which would make it less of an independent brake on activity.

For rate-sensitive borrowers, Logan argued that the expected path matters more for long-term rates than the exact timing of an individual increase. Gradual action during volatility could ease adjustment if markets understood the intended destination. Her proposed pause after two more moves would allow the committee to reassess both mandates. Changes in energy supply and conflict, AI-related investment or fiscal policy could alter the outlook. Long-run market and survey measures near 2% suggested confidence in the target, even while short-run expectations contributed to her judgment that prevailing policy was accommodative.

questions.question: How much of the rise in long Treasury yields reflects the expected policy path?
questions.detail: Logan attributed much of the move to stronger nominal growth and a higher neutral rate. That interpretation affects whether higher yields already restrain financing sufficiently and how a further increase would affect duration positions. Compare the contemporaneous Treasury curve, policy-rate futures, inflation compensation, rate surveys and term-premium estimates, especially around growth releases and the October meeting. Separate the expected short-rate path from compensation for uncertainty.

questions.question: How robust is the estimated shortfall of the policy rate below neutral?
questions.detail: Her calculation combines a 3.1% composite of short-horizon inflation expectations with a range of model-based neutral rates. Examine the underlying household, business and professional surveys and the eight models’ published inputs. Compare definitions, forecast horizons and the sensitivity to alternative expectations before estimating the real stance. A smaller gap would weaken the case for the same number of increases even if activity remained resilient.

questions.question: Will inflation remain broad after energy and tariff effects fade?
questions.detail: Growth in core services outside housing and transportation supported Logan’s forecast, while the trimmed mean indicated less pressure. Use the BEA’s detailed PCE releases, the Dallas Fed’s trimmed-mean components, wage agreements and official compensation data to test how widely prices and wages are accelerating. A persistent broadening would support a restrictive stance. Concentration in a few components would matter for the expected duration of that stance.
